body:
Follow up to #5851. Changes the default of the `JLD2Writer` `compress` keyword from `true` (the `Deflate` filter) to `[JLD2.Shuffle(), JLD2.ZstdFilter(1)]`: byte shuffling followed by Zstandard compression at level 1. Both filters are lossless, so the data read back is bit-for-bit what was written.

`compress = true`, `compress = false`, a single filter, or any vector of filters can still be passed, as before.

## Why

Benchmarks on Breeze.jl docs output comparing the current default with the new one. The `Deflate` numbers are from [the first sweep](https://github.com/CliMA/Oceananigans.jl/pull/5891#issuecomment-5385654336) and the `Shuffle` + Zstd numbers from [the sweep with `Shuffle`](https://github.com/CliMA/Oceananigans.jl/pull/5891#issuecomment-5394214322):

| file | uncompressed | `Deflate` (current) size / write / read | `Shuffle` + Zstd(1) size / write / read |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mountain_waves.jld2` | 6.4 MB | 4.6 MB / 0.11 s / 0.019 s | 4.2 MB / 0.025 s / 0.005 s |
| `cloudy_thermal_bubble.jld2` | 41.6 MB | 20.9 MB / 0.71 s / 0.10 s | 23.1 MB / 0.11 s / 0.028 s |
| `baroclinic_wave_k16.jld2` | 138.7 MB | 106.1 MB / 3.3 s / 0.43 s | 88.5 MB / 0.26 s / 0.12 s |
| `tc_rainband.jld2` | 955.6 MB | 653.6 MB / 25.8 s / 3.3 s | 514.3 MB / 2.3 s / 0.48 s |

Writes are about 4.5–13× faster and reads about 3.5–7× faster. Files are smaller in all cases except `cloudy_thermal_bubble.jld2`, which is about 11% larger.

- **Why `Shuffle`:** Zstd alone gave mixed results: faster, but some files were larger than with `Deflate` (e.g. `baroclinic_wave_k16.jld2`: 113 MB vs 106 MB). Shuffling the bytes of each value first makes the data much more compressible for both algorithms. Thanks to @nhz2 for the suggestion.
- **Why level 1:** higher levels compress only slightly better but write much slower. On `tc_rainband.jld2` with `Shuffle`, level 1 gives 514 MB in 2.3 s, level 3 gives 517 MB in 3.8 s, and level 19 gives 500 MB in 60 s.

## Compat

JLD2 compat is raised to `0.6.7` in `Project.toml` and `test/Project.toml`:

- JuliaIO/JLD2.jl#739 (v0.6.6) makes `ZstdFilter` respect the requested level; before that, level 1 was ignored.
- JuliaIO/JLD2.jl#740 (v0.6.7) makes `Shuffle` over 10× faster. Without it, writes with `Shuffle` are much slower.

## Not in this PR

Lossy compression, such as bitrounding the mantissa as @milankl suggested, would shrink files far more. It's left for a separate discussion about whether a lossy default is desirable; this PR stays lossless.
title: Switch default JLD2Writer compression to Shuffle + Zstd

body:
Recover the performance drop observed at https://github.com/NumericalEarth/Breeze.jl/pull/1097#pullrequestreview-5658505118.

> #6212 converted the regularization ϵ to the type of the global smoothness indicator τ, so the ZWENO weights of a BFloat16 scheme went from Float32 to BFloat16. BFloat16 has no approximate reciprocal instruction, so on CUDA the divisions in the weights fall back on inv (#6344) rather than the approximate Float32 reciprocal. The scalar tendency of a WENO5 BFloat16 scheme on a 256×256×128 grid on an RTX 5090 fell from 52.7e9 to 46.0e9 points/s, which the Breeze.jl benchmarks also caught.
> 
> The regularization of Float32 and BFloat16 schemes is now Float32, which makes their weights Float32 as before #6212. Near a Bounded boundary the reconstruction falls back on lower-order buffer schemes whose last one is BFloat16, so the buffer result is converted to the type of the high-order one, which keeps the interpolation type-stable. BFloat16 WENO5, WENO7 and WENO9 scalar tendencies are now 41%, 36% and 40% faster, 23% faster than before #6212 for WENO5, and Float32 is unchanged.

labels.description: So we can get the wrong answer even faster
labels.name: performance 🏍️

labels.description: Where Oceananigans gets its powers from
labels.name: GPU 👾

title: Compute the WENO weights of BFloat16 schemes in Float32

body:
This is step number (2a) of the roadmap laid out in #6272. It introduces an `Open` topology which is conceptually different from a `Closed` topology. While the latter has a wall, therefore (following the roadmap) has no physical halos beyond the wall and no operators will look beyond the wall, an `Open` topology has physical halos and operators will be allowed to look at halos beyond `Open` directions as if they were part of the domain.

A follow-up which moves the update of prognostic open BCs (`Radiation`, `PerturbationAdvection`, ....) once per stage rather than in the `fill_halo_regions!` will follow this PR.

A summary of new behavior when specifying topologies is in https://github.com/CliMA/Oceananigans.jl/pull/6276#issuecomment-6364806652

labels.description: Concerning a change which breaks the API
labels.name: breaking change :broken_heart:

title: (0.117.0) Introduce an `Open` topology
